body:
# Macha — the one true spelling, and the forms that fail it

*A letter to a colleague, 31 July 2026 — on the name Macha, and on the forms that keep failing it.*

Your note said, roughly: surely the marks are a nicety. Permit me to use Macha to show they are not.

First, the attestation. The tradition's record preserves this name in its romanized scholarly form: **Macha** — no older script survives to transcribe, so the canonical content is the exactness of the spelling itself.

Say it aloud as the sources heard it: 'MAHKH-ah' — two short open a's, stress on the first, and let the ch rasp like the end of Scottish 'loch'. Modern Irish keeps the sound: Eamhain Mhacha is said with the same fricative. The marks are what carry that sound to a reader who has never heard it spoken.

On the plain form — and I want to be precise, because you pushed on this. The plain form *macha* differs from the canonical *Macha* only by convention of display — case, not content. It is *acceptable everywhere*: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

One more thing, because it always surprises: the name did not stay home. Macha's clearest cross-border witness is Welsh, and it is the standard comparison of the handbooks: [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]] of the First Branch of the Mabinogi, the otherworld woman on the horse no rider can overtake, who — falsely accused and shamed — is sentenced to sit at the horse-block and offer to carry guests on her back like a beast of burden.  Mac Cana and Sjoestedt both set the two figures side by side: the sovereignty woman bound to horses, wronged by the men of the court, and made to bear an equine humiliation.

And it never stopped working. Macha rode the Celtic revival as the first wrong of the Ulster Cycle.  Lady Gregory's Cuchulain of Muirthemne (1902) opens the epic with her — 'The Curse of Macha' — and made the race and the debility the gateway through which two generations of English readers entered the Táin.

## The Convention's Own History

Every tradition in this register has its own scholarly transliteration standard, built by its own specialists over decades or centuries, and the register follows each on its own terms: the tradition’s own standard. The principle that unifies them is the one the whole project stands on: a name is evidence, and evidence is not negotiable — not for keyboards, not for convenience, not for anyone.

## Where Protocol Meets Practice

The technical answer is simple: the canonical marks are legal IDNA 2008 characters, encoded as punycode under `xn--`. The practical answer is messier: legal does not mean stocked (registrar inventory is partial), and stocked does not mean typeable (stacked diacritics defeat mobile keyboards).

So the register's rule is a hierarchy of attested forms — full restoration, circumflex, macron-only, attested variant, and finally plain ASCII for the systems that cannot carry marks. Every rung is defensible because every rung is attested. The forms this register rules against are not rungs; they are errors, and errors do not get rungs.

Write back when you have checked the sources; they are better company than I am.

*— The Register*

## The Verdict

**Macha** is the canonical form: attested, checkable, and enforced across the temple, the lexicon, the cards, the APIs, and this register. The plain form *macha* shares that standing — the two are the same name in every system. The false forms above are documented so that no reader has to take the temple's word on faith — the violations are stated, the sources are named, and the register stands open to challenge on every line.

The temple of **Macha** stands at [/macha/](/macha/).

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 12 cited sources — Noínden Ulad (The Debility of the Ulaidians), ed. Vernam Hull, Celtica 8 (1968) — the woman at Cruinniuc's door; the race, the twins, and the curse, Táin Bó Cúailnge, Recension 1, ed. and trans. Cecile O'Rahilly (Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies, 1976) — the ces noínden in the epic; mesrad Machae, 'Macha's mast', Lebor Gabála Érenn, ed. and trans. R. A. S. Macalister (Irish Texts Society, 1938–56) — Macha wife of Nemed; Macha Mongrúad daughter of Áed Rúad; the three daughters of Ernmas.
